newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong handover still not sold out.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong handover still not sold out.

text.p: After all the hype about Hong Kong's handover to China, airlines and hotels still have space for customers.
Last-minute flights to Hong Kong are available, mainly in economy. So, too, are hotel rooms with a harbour view of Monday evening's epic celebration marking the handover.
An informal survey of airlines and hotels serving Hong Kong shows that their business has fallen short of the sell-out confidently predicted for the past several months.
"There has been less demand for inbound airline seats than expected for a couple of reasons," explained Christopher Luk, programme marketing manager for Northwest Airlines in Hong Kong.

"One reason is that Hong Kong's chief executive-designate (Tung Chee-hwa) has made it clear there is no reason for expatriate Chinese to rush in from Canada and the United States to preserve their residency right."
"Then there's the "Olympics effect" surrounding heavily promoted events like the handover. People decide it's more bother than it's worth to try to get to the event, and they stay home."
Luk said Northwest had expected its Hong Kong-bound flights to be full but they were flying instead at 80 per cent capacity.
The Hong Kong Hotel Association says the occupancy rate for handover night among its members is about 93 per cent.
Hong Kong's most expensive hotels, such as the world-famous Penninsula in Kowloon which took its first handover registration in 1988, have been fully booked for several years.
But a telephone poll indicated rooms were still available on both sides of the harbour, even in luxury-class establishments.
The Excelsior on Hong Kong island has harbour-view rooms for $HK3,497 (US$450) per night, including on handover night.
Most first and business class seats are booked on airlines flying into Hong Kong from Europe, North America and Asia between now and the handover. But economy seats are available.
"It has been obvious for a couple of months now that the attractiveness of the handover event itself may have been oversold," said Ian Perkin, chief economist for the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce.
"Several months ago the industry was saying things were fully booked. That was on the basis of block bookings made in the belief that people would come. The hype may have driven some people away."
One group which lived up to expectations is the world's press. About 8,000 journalists applied for press credentials to cover the handover, and 5,100 have so far picked up passes.

Hong Kong will be on holiday for five consecutive days over the long handover weekend from Saturday. The markets and banks will be closed until Thursday but other businesses in the territory's largely unregulated economy can open if they choose.
Hong Kong's telephone company has no doubt about the impact of the handover on its business.

"Any time there's a major social event like this people pick up the phone and call friends and family," said Hongkong Telecom's Kim Yu. "You could say this is like having a 13th month of business for us."
